title: Chapter 62 — Contract Pricing Discipline, Net Terms & Credit
intro: Holding contract pricing under pressure, net terms, credit risk, and the receivables conversation.

sections.title: Pricing Discipline
sections.content:
Trade pricing is a commitment. When you quote a builder a price for a project, that price should hold for the duration of the project — typically 3-6 months. Do not requote at higher prices mid-project. That destroys trust faster than anything else.

Know your margin guidelines for trade accounts. The volume makes up for the per-unit margin compression. A builder account at 22 percent margin on 50 units per year is more profitable than retail at 28 percent margin on 15 units.

sections.title: Net Terms and Credit
sections.content:
Established trade accounts often expect net-30 or net-60 payment terms. This is normal in B2B. But it creates credit risk.

Before extending terms, check the account's payment history. A builder who pays on time for six months has earned net-30. A new account gets deposits until they prove reliability.

The receivables conversation is uncomfortable but necessary. 'I noticed your last two invoices are at 45 days. Our terms are net-30. Can we get current? I want to keep your priority delivery status.'

sections.title: Protecting the Relationship
sections.content:
The hardest part of trade pricing is saying no to discount requests that go beyond your margin floor. 'I understand you are comparing prices. Here is what I can do within our program. I cannot go lower without compromising the service level that makes our partnership work.'

Never compete on price alone with trade accounts. Compete on service, reliability, and expertise. The builder who leaves for a $200 savings on a $5,000 order will come back when the cheaper supplier misses a delivery and delays their project by a week.
